The total amount of injected argon was 7.39x10^20 atoms for the carbon wall case (#79423) and 5.68x10^20 atoms for the ILW case (#81928), a 30% higher amount in the carbon wall case.
The current quench time was 18.6 ms for the carbon wall case (#79423) and 35.0 ms for the ILW case (#81928), indicating a significantly slower current quench in the ILW discharge.
In the carbon wall case (#79423), a runaway electron plateau of 600 kA was observed, while in the ILW case (#81928) the runaway current was negligibly small (less than 70 kA).

In the ILW case, the temperature dropped during the thermal quench but then recovered to around 300 eV, followed by a slow drop, while in the carbon wall case the temperature dropped continuously down to 10 eV after the thermal quench.

The numerical modeling showed that the differences in runaway electron generation were due to a complex, combined effect of differences in plasma parameter profiles, radiation characteristics, and injected argon amount between the two cases.
The modeling included scans of argon and background impurity (carbon or beryllium) content, as these quantities were extremely hard to accurately determine experimentally during the disruption.
The paper noted that hot tail generation was not expected to be important in these cases, as the cooling times were long enough for Dreicer generation to dominate over hot-tail generation.
Radial diffusion due to magnetic perturbations was considered as a potential runaway loss mechanism, but the specific level of perturbations needed for suppression was not determined.
The pre-disruption Zeff was 2.2 ± 20% for the carbon wall case and 2.5 ± 20% for the ILW case, indicating a relatively high impurity content in the ILW discharge.

The numerical model (GO code) calculated the evolution of the impurity density, ionization, recombination, and radiation, coupled to the plasma temperature, density, and current evolution, in order to self-consistently simulate the disruption dynamics.
